{"selected_source_ids":["D01","D02","D03","D04","D05","D06","D07","D08","D10","D12","D13","D14","D19"],"excluded_sources":[{"source_id":"D09","reason":"anchor_or_prohibited"},{"source_id":"D11","reason":"task_irrelevant"},{"source_id":"D12","reason":"review_or_nonprimary"},{"source_id":"D13","reason":"review_or_nonprimary"},{"source_id":"D14","reason":"review_or_nonprimary"},{"source_id":"D15","reason":"task_irrelevant"},{"source_id":"D16","reason":"task_irrelevant"},{"source_id":"D17","reason":"task_irrelevant"},{"source_id":"D18","reason":"review_or_nonprimary"},{"source_id":"D20","reason":"task_irrelevant"}],"selection_rationale":"Most selected documents are experimental or field/pilot studies on regeneration or destruction of PFAS-loaded adsorption media (activated carbon, ion exchange resins, engineered sorbents) and report quantitative data on desorption, recovered capacity, repeated cycles, media deterioration, and residual streams (D01–D08, D10, D14). Several works provide life-cycle and techno‑economic modeling of regeneration vs single‑use/thermal reactivation/disposal scenarios, directly informing operational, energy, chemical, cost, and sustainability trade‑offs (D06, D12, D13, D19). D07 gives primary experimental evidence on supercritical water oxidation of spent media, including PFAS elimination and residual characterization, addressing end‑of‑life destruction.

Excluded cards are either reviews (D18) or likely the defining review for this task (D09), or they focus on adsorption materials without providing primary data on regeneration or end‑of‑life management (D11), or they treat PFAS in matrices or processes not centered on adsorption media management (US/persulfate in water/soil, foam fractionation, EO treatment trains) and thus fall outside the specific task boundary on PFAS‑loaded adsorption media (D15, D16, D17, D20). At least six strong, independent primary sources remain, covering all required components, so the minimum‑evidence gate is satisfied.","component_coverage":[{"component_id":"RT03-C1","selected_source_ids":["D01","D02","D03","D04","D05","D06","D08","D10","D14"],"rationale":"These sources provide primary data on regeneration of PFAS-loaded adsorbents and ion exchange resins, allowing comparison of regeneration approaches, recovered capacity, and multi‑cycle performance.
• D01: Regeneration of CTAB‑impregnated activated carbon for PFOA with multiple regenerants; quantifies PFOA desorption to regenerant and includes recovery of PFOA and regenerant, enabling assessment of regeneration efficiency and material reuse.
• D02: Cyclic IX removal and UV/sulfite destruction; reports PFAS recoveries during regeneration of PFA694E and IRA910 resins in different matrices, resin reuse over multiple cycles, and ties incomplete regeneration to eventual need for replacement.
• D03: Direct in‑situ chemical regeneration of IX resins using sulfate radical AOP; tracks PFOA removal, resin regeneration, and fluoride formation over multiple adsorption–regeneration cycles, plus resin characterization.
• D04: Short‑chain PFAS removal using GAC and AER; includes batch and column regeneration tests with various regenerants (NaOH, NaCl/ethanol, HCl/ethanol), PFAS mass balances, and multiple regeneration cycles.
• D05: Regenerable activated carbon and biochar for simultaneous PFAS and Cd(II) removal; compares different washing strategies (methanol, HCl, sequential), reports regeneration efficiencies and adsorption performance over three cycles.
• D06: Regeneration of conventional and PFAS‑selective AERs; systematically screens regenerant compositions (brine/organic cosolvent), reports desorption efficiencies, restored capacities, and performance of regenerated resins, with discussion of field‑loaded media and multiple potential cycles.
• D08: IX removal of emerging PFAS and regeneration; evaluates practical regeneration conditions (brine strength, solvent fraction), PFAS‑specific recovery, and extent to which resin capacity is restored across resins.
• D10: Regeneration of a PVA‑CTAC electrospun nanofiber membrane; uses methanolic ammonium hydroxide regenerant and shows PFAS removal efficiencies and any decline over three adsorption‑desorption cycles, indicating material durability.
• D14: Pilot comparison of regenerable vs single‑use AERs; provides column loading behavior, PFAS mass distributions within spent resins, and implications for resin utilization and regeneration strategy, informing when regeneration vs replacement is advantageous."},{"component_id":"RT03-C2","selected_source_ids":["D01","D02","D03","D06","D07","D08","D12","D13","D14","D19"],"rationale":"These works explicitly treat PFAS mass balances and fate in regeneration streams, spent media, or destructive processes, enabling distinction between PFAS transfer and actual destruction, and characterizing liquid, gaseous, and solid residuals.
• D01: Quantifies PFOA released into regenerant and then recovered, with mass balance for PFOA and regenerant components; clearly illustrates that regeneration transfers PFAS to liquid regenerant and later to a recovered PFOA product, not destruction.
• D02: For IX plus UV/sulfite, details PFAS recoveries in regenerant, PFAS partitioning during distillation (still bottoms vs condensate), and nearly complete defluorination for most PFAS during UV/sulfite; explicitly separates capture, regeneration, and destructive polishing and highlights remaining short‑chain PFAS.
• D03: Measures fluoride release during sulfate radical regeneration of IX, enabling quantification of PFAS transformation and distinguishing mineralization from mere desorption; compares conditions with and without oxidant.
• D06: Discusses PFAS in regenerant brines and the role of cosolvent recovery via distillation, including concerns over PFAS volatility and potential back‑contamination; links regenerant composition to downstream management requirements and LCA impacts.
• D07: SCWO treatment of GAC and AIX spent media; reports PFAS elimination efficiencies for individual PFAS classes, notes discrepancies in PFAS mass recovery from spent GAC vs operational loading, and addresses analytical recovery limitations; characterizes residual PFAS in effluents and hence degree of destruction vs residual contamination.
• D08: Quantifies PFAS mass desorbed into brine/solvent regenerants and shows dependence on PFAS and resin type, clearly demonstrating that conventional regeneration mainly transfers PFAS to concentrated liquid waste.
• D12: LCA of AER regeneration options; explicitly models regeneration waste streams (spent regenerant, distillation still bottoms, incineration) and their environmental burdens, even assuming idealized 100% desorption, clarifying that environmental impacts shift among waste forms and processes.
• D13: Comparative LCA/LCCA of AER (with on‑site regeneration) versus GAC (with off‑site incineration or thermal reactivation); captures emissions and residual streams associated with regenerant handling, incineration, and reactivation of spent media.
• D14: Extracts PFAS from spent resins and examines spatial distribution along columns; while not a regeneration test per se, it quantifies PFAS still immobilized in spent media versus those displaced into effluent, highlighting how operational strategy affects PFAS in solids vs treated water.
• D19: Technoeconomic/design analysis for WRRF PFAS treatment that contrasts single‑use GAC/AIX plus off‑site reactivation/HTI with destruction‑oriented options; discusses implications for changeout frequency, residual management pathways (e.g., incineration, high‑temperature treatment), and emphasizes that capture technologies alone do not destroy PFAS."},{"component_id":"RT03-C3","selected_source_ids":["D02","D05","D06","D07","D10","D12","D13","D19"],"rationale":"These studies collectively provide the operational, energy, chemical, cost, and broader sustainability evidence needed for site‑specific decisions between regenerating, replacing, or destructively treating PFAS‑loaded media.
• D02: Evaluates a treatment train combining IX adsorption, regenerant distillation, and UV/sulfite destruction; discusses regenerant reuse, impacts of solvent composition, and trade‑offs between resin type (PFAS‑selective vs generic) in terms of regeneration ease and overall treatment feasibility, with implications for operational cost and complexity.
• D05: Investigates low‑temperature, chemical‑based regeneration strategies for carbonaceous sorbents, comparing methanol, acid, and sequential methanol/acid washing, with implications for chemical consumption, separate handling of PFAS vs metals, and the practicality of multi‑contaminant sorbent reuse.
• D06: Presents experimental regeneration performance and couples it to a brief life‑cycle and cost assessment comparing AER systems with regenerant recovery versus alternatives. It quantifies how regenerant composition, cosolvent recovery (distillation energy), and number of regeneration cycles affect system‑level environmental impacts and costs.
• D07: Provides SCWO operating parameters and PFAS destruction efficiencies for spent media treatment, informing energy intensity and effectiveness of an end‑of‑life destructive option for GAC and AIX relative to off‑site incineration or long‑term disposal.
• D10: Details a practical regeneration protocol (methanolic NH4OH, CTAC reconditioning, drying) for an electrospun membrane and shows stable performance over cycles, illustrating the operational steps, chemicals, and durability considerations for a regenerable engineered sorbent.
• D12: An LCA specifically on AER regeneration options, dissecting contributions from methanol distillation, salt production, electricity, and waste disposal (including incineration scenarios). It provides parametric insight into how regenerant selection and waste handling change climate, toxicity, and other impact categories per m³ treated.
• D13: Joint LCA/LCCA comparing single‑use vs regenerable AER and GAC systems, including off‑site incineration and thermal reactivation. It quantifies media usage rates, breakthrough‑criteria‑dependent changeout frequencies, energy use, transport, and costs, providing a framework for site‑specific selection of regeneration vs replacement vs reactivation.
• D19: Develops preliminary designs and cost estimates for PFAS removal and destruction options at WRRFs (GAC, AIX, reactivation, high‑temperature incineration / HTI), emphasizing how influent quality, treatment goals, existing infrastructure, and distance to reactivation/destruction facilities drive capital and O&M costs and feasible management pathways. This directly informs how utilities might choose between regenerating media, replacing and reactivating off‑site, or adopting destructive treatment at different scales."}]}

You are selecting primary PFAS treatment studies for a focused professional
review. You receive one task and an anonymized, BGE-ranked list of candidate
document cards.

Classify every candidate card. Select every document that is an independent
primary study, is directly relevant to at least one task component, and
contains extractable decision-relevant evidence. There is no target number of
selected documents and no penalty for retaining all eligible studies.

Eligible evidence includes:

- primary experiments, pilot or field deployments, and quantitative modeling
  or life-cycle studies;
- complementary matrices, PFAS scopes, operating regimes, endpoints, and
  scales;
- documents with concrete methods, conditions, results, limitations, residuals,
  energy, or cost evidence; and
- evidence that permits meaningful comparison or explains non-comparability.

Do not select a document merely because its title repeats task words. Do not
select reviews, perspectives, reference lists, duplicate records, or the
held-out defining review. Do not exclude an otherwise eligible study merely
because another selected study reports similar findings. Do not infer facts
absent from a card. Selection is document-level only: do not write the review
and do not score candidate answers.

Every candidate source_id must appear exactly once, either in
selected_source_ids or excluded_sources. Each required component must be
covered by at least one selected source. Return selected_source_ids in BGE rank
order.

Return one JSON object following the supplied schema exactly.

Required components:
[{"component_id":"RT03-C1","requirement":"Compare regeneration approaches by PFAS release or destruction, recovered capacity, repeated-cycle performance, and material deterioration."},{"component_id":"RT03-C2","requirement":"Account for liquid, gaseous, or solid residuals and distinguish transfer of PFAS from actual destruction."},{"component_id":"RT03-C3","requirement":"Evaluate the operational, energy, chemical, cost, and sustainability evidence needed for a site-specific decision."}]

Task boundaries:
{"constraints":[{"constraint_id":"RT03-B1","material_violation_rule":"Triggers if desorption or recovered adsorption capacity is called PFAS destruction without direct transformation or fluorine-endpoint evidence."},{"constraint_id":"RT03-B2","material_violation_rule":"Triggers if a management option is called sustainable based only on one regeneration cycle while ignoring material deterioration, energy, chemicals, emissions, or secondary waste."}],"required_component_ids":["RT03-C1","RT03-C2","RT03-C3"],"task_boundaries":"Regeneration, replacement, and end-of-life management of PFAS-loaded adsorption media and all resulting residual streams.","task_id":"RT03"}

component_coverage.rationale:
These sources provide primary data on regeneration of PFAS-loaded adsorbents and ion exchange resins, allowing comparison of regeneration approaches, recovered capacity, and multi‑cycle performance.
• D01: Regeneration of CTAB‑impregnated activated carbon for PFOA with multiple regenerants; quantifies PFOA desorption to regenerant and includes recovery of PFOA and regenerant, enabling assessment of regeneration efficiency and material reuse.
• D02: Cyclic IX removal and UV/sulfite destruction; reports PFAS recoveries during regeneration of PFA694E and IRA910 resins in different matrices, resin reuse over multiple cycles, and ties incomplete regeneration to eventual need for replacement.
• D03: Direct in‑situ chemical regeneration of IX resins using sulfate radical AOP; tracks PFOA removal, resin regeneration, and fluoride formation over multiple adsorption–regeneration cycles, plus resin characterization.
• D04: Short‑chain PFAS removal using GAC and AER; includes batch and column regeneration tests with various regenerants (NaOH, NaCl/ethanol, HCl/ethanol), PFAS mass balances, and multiple regeneration cycles.
• D05: Regenerable activated carbon and biochar for simultaneous PFAS and Cd(II) removal; compares different washing strategies (methanol, HCl, sequential), reports regeneration efficiencies and adsorption performance over three cycles.
• D06: Regeneration of conventional and PFAS‑selective AERs; systematically screens regenerant compositions (brine/organic cosolvent), reports desorption efficiencies, restored capacities, and performance of regenerated resins, with discussion of field‑loaded media and multiple potential cycles.
• D08: IX removal of emerging PFAS and regeneration; evaluates practical regeneration conditions (brine strength, solvent fraction), PFAS‑specific recovery, and extent to which resin capacity is restored across resins.
• D10: Regeneration of a PVA‑CTAC electrospun nanofiber membrane; uses methanolic ammonium hydroxide regenerant and shows PFAS removal efficiencies and any decline over three adsorption‑desorption cycles, indicating material durability.
• D14: Pilot comparison of regenerable vs single‑use AERs; provides column loading behavior, PFAS mass distributions within spent resins, and implications for resin utilization and regeneration strategy, informing when regeneration vs replacement is advantageous.

These works explicitly treat PFAS mass balances and fate in regeneration streams, spent media, or destructive processes, enabling distinction between PFAS transfer and actual destruction, and characterizing liquid, gaseous, and solid residuals.
• D01: Quantifies PFOA released into regenerant and then recovered, with mass balance for PFOA and regenerant components; clearly illustrates that regeneration transfers PFAS to liquid regenerant and later to a recovered PFOA product, not destruction.
• D02: For IX plus UV/sulfite, details PFAS recoveries in regenerant, PFAS partitioning during distillation (still bottoms vs condensate), and nearly complete defluorination for most PFAS during UV/sulfite; explicitly separates capture, regeneration, and destructive polishing and highlights remaining short‑chain PFAS.
• D03: Measures fluoride release during sulfate radical regeneration of IX, enabling quantification of PFAS transformation and distinguishing mineralization from mere desorption; compares conditions with and without oxidant.
• D06: Discusses PFAS in regenerant brines and the role of cosolvent recovery via distillation, including concerns over PFAS volatility and potential back‑contamination; links regenerant composition to downstream management requirements and LCA impacts.
• D07: SCWO treatment of GAC and AIX spent media; reports PFAS elimination efficiencies for individual PFAS classes, notes discrepancies in PFAS mass recovery from spent GAC vs operational loading, and addresses analytical recovery limitations; characterizes residual PFAS in effluents and hence degree of destruction vs residual contamination.
• D08: Quantifies PFAS mass desorbed into brine/solvent regenerants and shows dependence on PFAS and resin type, clearly demonstrating that conventional regeneration mainly transfers PFAS to concentrated liquid waste.
• D12: LCA of AER regeneration options; explicitly models regeneration waste streams (spent regenerant, distillation still bottoms, incineration) and their environmental burdens, even assuming idealized 100% desorption, clarifying that environmental impacts shift among waste forms and processes.
• D13: Comparative LCA/LCCA of AER (with on‑site regeneration) versus GAC (with off‑site incineration or thermal reactivation); captures emissions and residual streams associated with regenerant handling, incineration, and reactivation of spent media.
• D14: Extracts PFAS from spent resins and examines spatial distribution along columns; while not a regeneration test per se, it quantifies PFAS still immobilized in spent media versus those displaced into effluent, highlighting how operational strategy affects PFAS in solids vs treated water.
• D19: Technoeconomic/design analysis for WRRF PFAS treatment that contrasts single‑use GAC/AIX plus off‑site reactivation/HTI with destruction‑oriented options; discusses implications for changeout frequency, residual management pathways (e.g., incineration, high‑temperature treatment), and emphasizes that capture technologies alone do not destroy PFAS.

These studies collectively provide the operational, energy, chemical, cost, and broader sustainability evidence needed for site‑specific decisions between regenerating, replacing, or destructively treating PFAS‑loaded media.
• D02: Evaluates a treatment train combining IX adsorption, regenerant distillation, and UV/sulfite destruction; discusses regenerant reuse, impacts of solvent composition, and trade‑offs between resin type (PFAS‑selective vs generic) in terms of regeneration ease and overall treatment feasibility, with implications for operational cost and complexity.
• D05: Investigates low‑temperature, chemical‑based regeneration strategies for carbonaceous sorbents, comparing methanol, acid, and sequential methanol/acid washing, with implications for chemical consumption, separate handling of PFAS vs metals, and the practicality of multi‑contaminant sorbent reuse.
• D06: Presents experimental regeneration performance and couples it to a brief life‑cycle and cost assessment comparing AER systems with regenerant recovery versus alternatives. It quantifies how regenerant composition, cosolvent recovery (distillation energy), and number of regeneration cycles affect system‑level environmental impacts and costs.
• D07: Provides SCWO operating parameters and PFAS destruction efficiencies for spent media treatment, informing energy intensity and effectiveness of an end‑of‑life destructive option for GAC and AIX relative to off‑site incineration or long‑term disposal.
• D10: Details a practical regeneration protocol (methanolic NH4OH, CTAC reconditioning, drying) for an electrospun membrane and shows stable performance over cycles, illustrating the operational steps, chemicals, and durability considerations for a regenerable engineered sorbent.
• D12: An LCA specifically on AER regeneration options, dissecting contributions from methanol distillation, salt production, electricity, and waste disposal (including incineration scenarios). It provides parametric insight into how regenerant selection and waste handling change climate, toxicity, and other impact categories per m³ treated.
• D13: Joint LCA/LCCA comparing single‑use vs regenerable AER and GAC systems, including off‑site incineration and thermal reactivation. It quantifies media usage rates, breakthrough‑criteria‑dependent changeout frequencies, energy use, transport, and costs, providing a framework for site‑specific selection of regeneration vs replacement vs reactivation.
• D19: Develops preliminary designs and cost estimates for PFAS removal and destruction options at WRRFs (GAC, AIX, reactivation, high‑temperature incineration / HTI), emphasizing how influent quality, treatment goals, existing infrastructure, and distance to reactivation/destruction facilities drive capital and O&M costs and feasible management pathways. This directly informs how utilities might choose between regenerating media, replacing and reactivating off‑site, or adopting destructive treatment at different scales.

result.selection_rationale:
Most selected documents are experimental or field/pilot studies on regeneration or destruction of PFAS-loaded adsorption media (activated carbon, ion exchange resins, engineered sorbents) and report quantitative data on desorption, recovered capacity, repeated cycles, media deterioration, and residual streams (D01–D08, D10, D14). Several works provide life-cycle and techno‑economic modeling of regeneration vs single‑use/thermal reactivation/disposal scenarios, directly informing operational, energy, chemical, cost, and sustainability trade‑offs (D06, D12, D13, D19). D07 gives primary experimental evidence on supercritical water oxidation of spent media, including PFAS elimination and residual characterization, addressing end‑of‑life destruction.

Excluded cards are either reviews (D18) or likely the defining review for this task (D09), or they focus on adsorption materials without providing primary data on regeneration or end‑of‑life management (D11), or they treat PFAS in matrices or processes not centered on adsorption media management (US/persulfate in water/soil, foam fractionation, EO treatment trains) and thus fall outside the specific task boundary on PFAS‑loaded adsorption media (D15, D16, D17, D20). At least six strong, independent primary sources remain, covering all required components, so the minimum‑evidence gate is satisfied.
